1:
Chrysostom explains why the argument stands here. Paul had said he would eat no flesh for ever rather than make his brother stumble, a thing he had not yet done; lest anyone answer that promises are easy and bid him show by deeds, he is compelled to prove it. Chrysostom then raises the stake: it is admirable that he abstained from things lawful, but the admirable part is his doing so at the cost of much trouble and danger. Calvin argues the same from equity, that whatever law a man imposes on others he should submit to himself; Paul had promised, but since a promise for the future might not be believed, he points to what he had already done. Henry adds that it is no strange nor new thing for a minister to meet unkind returns for great good-will, and Clarke that the highest proof of Paul's disinterested benevolence was produced by his opponents as an argument against him. Barnes sets out the four charges he thinks lay behind the chapter: that Paul had not seen Christ, that he lived unlike the other apostles, that he and Barnabas laboured with their hands, and that his not claiming maintenance showed he knew he had no right to it.

The opening words are disputed in order and in sense. Gill reports that the Syriac, Ethiopic and Vulgate put the clause about freedom first, as does the Alexandrian copy, and that many think this the better order, the argument then rising from the less to the greater. Ellicott prefers the same order on manuscript grounds and finds the thought grows more naturally out of the preceding chapter, since Paul had given up one freedom about meat and another about maintenance, and the Jewish party inferred from the second that the right did not exist. What the freedom is Gill will not fix, offering liberty in things indifferent, freedom from the ceremonial law, or the right to a maintenance. Robertson takes the first sense and notes that all these questions expect an affirmative answer; Wesley reads the clauses as a rising scale, the liberty of a common Christian and then of an apostle.

On the sight of the Lord the accounts differ in number. Lightfoot says Paul saw him twice, on the road to Damascus when he was marked out for an apostle and in his trance at Jerusalem when he was marked out for the Gentiles, and adds that he alone among the apostles saw the Lord after the ascension. Robertson gathers half a dozen passages instead and observes that they qualify him though he was not one of the twelve. Ellicott names three occasions and infers from the question being asked and not answered that the fact was generally admitted.

The seal is where they divide over what the proof proves. Barnes will not call the conversion mere evidence but absolute proof, since Paul claimed the office among them and God owned the claim. Clarke turns antiquary, that the seal was a figure cut in a stone and set in a ring by which letters of credence were stamped, that the Greeks excelled at this engraving, and that the moderns contend in vain to rival them. Ellicott identifies the doubters as men who probably arrived at Corinth after Paul left and stirred up others to repudiate what they themselves did not acknowledge. Calvin alone sees that the argument might prove too much and puts the objection himself: does this not suit the false apostles equally, who also gather disciples? He answers that pure doctrine is required before any man may argue from his success, so impostors have no ground of congratulation though they deceive nations and kingdoms. Wesley adds what the seal included, that they received not only faith by his mouth but the gifts of the Spirit by his hands, and Robertson hears a pointed appeal for their support.
3:
The language of the defence is agreed to be forensic and disputed only as to direction. Barnes notes that the verb for examining is a court term used of judges, and suspects an allusion to the arrogance of men presuming to judge an apostle; Clarke has Paul questioned as upon oath; Ellicott calls both words technical terms of a tribunal; Robertson warns that the noun does not carry our sense of apologising, and adds that the critics at Corinth were investigating Paul with sharp eyes, as pastors are still kept under the critic's spy-glass. Whether the sentence looks backward or forward divides them: Gill, Clarke and Wesley attach it to what precedes, Ellicott says flatly it refers to what has gone before and not to what follows, and Robertson alone will have it both ways. Lightfoot supplies a motive none of the others give, that Paul was accused of taking maintenance from heathen churches, or watched by cavillers to see whether he would, and turned to mechanic labour to stop the mouths of the Jews who barked against him. Calvin turns the argument on the readers, that the Corinthians injure themselves by refusing the acknowledgment, since their faith and his apostleship stand or fall together.

The sister who is a wife is the controversy of the passage. Gill calls the phrase a Hebraism answering to the sister-spouse of the Canticles, and rejects the reading which makes her a rich woman ministering of her substance, since that would relieve the churches of the very charge Paul claims the right to lay on them. Clarke treats the verse as decisive against clerical celibacy, since the Lord's brethren were married and Peter certainly was, and their wives shared the faith, less being impossible in the word sister; he notes all the same that Clement said the apostles carried their wives not as wives but as sisters. Ellicott dismisses the Roman reading that Christian matrons attended the apostles as sisters, since the appeal to Peter makes it inadmissible, and records that a practice growing out of that misapprehension was condemned at the first council of Nicaea. Henry reaches the same conclusion from the word for power, which implies authority to require attendance, such as no man has over any but a wife or servant, and apostles who worked for their bread could keep no servants. Calvin meets the opposite excess, that Eusebius inferred Paul was married and had left his wife lest she burden the churches; there is no foundation for it, since he might urge the right without possessing it, and Robertson agrees that Paul plainly had no wife then. Barnes states the objection answered, that the two travelled without wives, from which their opponents inferred a conscious want of claim; Wesley draws from Peter that he lived with his wife after he became an apostle and had no right which was not equally Paul's.

The last question narrows to two men. Robertson observes that this is the first mention of Barnabas since the dispute at Antioch and that it is made in good spirit, the two having worked at their own charges on the first journey, Paul receiving no aid until Philippi. Barnes finds behind the singling out some peculiar spleen against them. Ellicott reads the word only as implying that all the rest did exercise the right, so the objection stands only by making an arbitrary exception of these two. Clarke draws two inferences instead, that the apostles did not generally support themselves by their labour and that these two did, having a trade they could carry anywhere. Calvin, provoked by the naming of Cephas, concedes that Peter was acknowledged first among the apostles, since every society needs one to preside, but insists the pre-eminence was not lordship and that the first place in one church is not dominion over the world.
7:
Three pictures from common life carry the first argument, and the commentators fill them in from history. Robertson traces the word for a soldier's pay to a term for cooked meat bought with bread, so that it meant rations before wages, and notes it is the word used of the wages of sin; Clarke adds that Roman soldiers were paid in victuals as well as money. Gill and Calvin both allow that men have served at their own charges, Gill naming the Habessines and the ancient Romans and dating the senate's act for a stipend before Paul wrote. Ellicott prefers the shorter reading in the third picture, that the vineyard owner eats his fruit while the keeper of a flock eats of the milk, since a man may eat fruit but is sustained by milk only through selling it. Robertson counts the whole series, soldier and husbandman and shepherd, the ox and the ploughman and the priests at the altar, calls it proof enough in all conscience, and remarks that it is still not enough for churches that starve their pastors in the name of piety.

Ellicott makes an observation that has nothing to do with the argument and is the more striking for it. Paul never takes up the image the Lord himself supplied, of Christ the Shepherd and the Church his flock, save once at Miletus; he does not take it up even here, where the word flock stood in his own sentence. Peter's favourite image is the flock, the command to feed it having made the figure touchingly familiar to him. Paul's pictures from country life run to the practical rather than the poetic.

The appeal then moves from common sense to the law, and the question is what the law was for. Barnes guards the inference, that Moses is not made to speak of the Christian ministry, only that the principle was settled there that a labourer should have his support, and that if God regarded a brute at work he would much more require provision for the ministers of religion. Calvin asks the question nobody else asks, why Paul chose this proof when clearer passages lay to hand, such as the command that the hireling's wages not remain overnight, and answers that there is more force in this one, since a requirement to care for cattle argues from the less to the greater about the equity God expects among men. Robertson notes that the objection Paul meets, that Scripture does not support paying preachers, is still made by the stingy.

The question about the oxen is read four ways. Barnes and Wesley both supply a word, asking whether God cares for oxen only, Wesley extending the principle to all the Mosaic laws of that kind. Clarke turns it into an argument from the lesser to the greater, that God is not likely to be solicitous for oxen and regardless of man, and then pushes it where no other voice here follows: God could not reprobate an ox since he careth for oxen, and surely cannot reprobate a man; and to the reply that a man has sinned and an ox cannot, he answers that the decree is supposed to be from eternity, and a man can no more sin before he exists than an ox can when he exists. Ellicott enters the opposite caution, that the words must not be taken as denying the divine regard for the brute creation, which runs through the Mosaic law and appears in the closing question of Jonah, but as stating the highest object of God's love. Robertson leaves the argument for the threshing-floor, where the Egyptians drove oxen over the grain dragging a sledge as they still do in Andalusia and Palestine, and quotes a hieroglyphic inscription bidding the oxen thresh measures of grain for themselves and measures for their masters. Gill contributes only the citation formula.
10:
How far the word altogether reaches is the first question here. Barnes denies flatly that it can mean the law was made solely for ministers, on three grounds: that this contradicts a law which had a real reference to oxen; that the argument does not require it; and that the word may be rendered chiefly or doubtless, as in several places of Luke and Acts. Gill leans the other way, that God delivered the law not merely for the ox but chiefly for men, citing Jarchi that the ox is named in order to express man, with a second Jewish authority reading the law of the bird's nest the same way.

The clause about ploughing and threshing is textually unsettled, and the four who notice it differ. Clarke reports that many of the best manuscripts give simply in hope of partaking, and quotes Pearce that the longer words are superfluous if not wrong, since men do not live in hope to partake of their hope but of what it was for; Griesbach left them out. Calvin describes the same double reading and then says the thing worth recording: were he at liberty to choose he would prefer the shorter, but since most Greek manuscripts agree in the other and the meaning is unaffected, he has not ventured to alter it. Ellicott settles for the sense that the plougher is bound to plough in hope and the thresher to thresh in hope of his share. Robertson observes what the others miss, that the two halves are not parallel, since the thresher may be the ox but the plougher can hardly be, every worker, beast or man, sharing in the fruit. Whether the picture is literal or spiritual Ellicott says has been much discussed; he takes it literally, as God's sanction upon the principle uniting labour with reward, the application to spiritual work following from the less to the greater.

That application comes next, and Calvin gets there by meeting a cavil. It might be said that ploughing and threshing yield fruit of the same kind as the labour, whereas gospel fruit is spiritual, so its minister ought to demand nothing carnal. He answers from the greater to the less: as the soul excels the body, so does the word of the Lord excel outward sustenance, and what injury is done if what is inestimable is recompensed with something small and contemptible? Ellicott hears a slight touch of sarcasm in the same movement, since the earlier argument established a labourer's right to payment in kind and Paul now asks only a reward as inferior to his work as carnal things are to spiritual. Gill expands the figure of sowing into the parable of the soils, the wayside, the stony who show affection without root, the thorny who are at first promising. Clarke reduces it to one right, that every man who preaches has a claim to his own support.

Who the others are is not settled. Gill allows either the false apostles or the true ministers there and Wesley says whether true or false; Barnes has no doubt the Corinthian teachers urged the right and received support, and Ellicott turns it into the argument, that since the Corinthians recognise the principle for others their first teachers have the stronger claim. On the enduring Barnes and Robertson agree in the etymology, the verb meaning to cover or keep off as a roof keeps off rain, and so to bear; Robertson adds that the word for hindrance means a cutting in and is very rare, and that Paul's care to avoid it rather than insist on his rights is an eloquent example for modern men. Clarke gives the motive plainly, lest any think they preached merely for a temporal support; Calvin turns it back on the readers, that the Corinthians should keep the same end in view, doing nothing that would retard the gospel.
13:
Chrysostom alone attends to the phrasing. Paul did not write that those who minister about sacred things receive from those who offer, but that they eat of the temple, so that neither the receivers may be blamed nor the givers lifted up; nor that those at the altar receive from the sacrificers, but that they have their portion with the altar, since what is offered belongs no longer to the offerer but to the temple. Nor did he say they receive the holy things, indicating their moderation and that they ought not to make money. The two classes are divided four ways. Barnes takes the first for the Levites and the second for the priests who offered sacrifice. Clarke widens the first to all the officers, priests and Levites and Nethinim alike, since the priests partook of the sacrifices while the rest lived on tithes and first fruits, it not being lawful for them to live on the sacrifices. Ellicott divides by the kind of support rather than the rank, the first clause covering maintenance from the offerings and the second the sacrificing priest's share of the animal. Lightfoot supplies rabbinic detail nobody else has, that among those who wrought in holy things without serving at the altar were the men who picked the worms out of the altar wood, blemished men unfit to minister there but nourished from the consecrated things; and he corrects the picture of waiting, since none but the king might sit within the court, so the word means rather besieging the altar. Gill and Ellicott agree in rejecting outright the reading that the priests meant are those of the heathen temples, which the Ethiopic version suggests and Ellicott calls wholly inadmissible.

The appeal to the Lord's own ordinance follows. Ellicott explains why the law is invoked twice, that it returns only to introduce the crowning argument, that Christ perpetuated the provision rather than abrogating it, and quotes Bengel's thrust that if the Mass were a sacrifice Paul would undoubtedly have fitted the second half of his sentence to it. Robertson judges that Paul, knowing the words of Jesus, has made the argument for a minister's salary complete for all time. Barnes at once limits what is granted, that the word is live and not grow rich, lay up treasures or speculate. Clarke matches it with a Jewish maxim, that the inhabitants of a town where a wise man dwelt should support him because he had forsaken the world's pleasures to study. Calvin uses the length of the argument for a rebuke, that the Corinthians deserved sharper handling for letting Christ's ministers be reviled in so justifiable a matter, though Paul touches it mildly so as to admonish without affronting.

The refusal in the last verse is put with a violence they all feel. Robertson says the tangled syntax reflects the intensity of Paul's feeling, notes the epistolary aorist by which he denies that he is hinting for a change, and marks the violent break where the expected infinitive gives way to a bare future. Ellicott reports a great variety of readings and more than one reconstruction of the broken sentence. Henry defines the glorying so it will not be mistaken: it implies nothing of boasting or catching at applause but a high degree of satisfaction, and Paul valued his advantages for promoting the gospel above his rights and his life. Calvin gives the reason for the vehemence, that the authority of the gospel in some degree depended on it and a handle would otherwise have been given to the false apostles. Barnes adds that his labouring with his own hands had itself been urged as proof that he was no apostle; Gill lists what he had foregone, and Clarke and Wesley close briefly, that he does not write to lay in his claim and would rather die than give occasion to those who seek it.
16:
Barnes opens by admitting these three verses are very difficult and variously understood, and states the problem: glorying must attach to something voluntary, yet a necessity is laid on Paul, so the ground of reward must lie elsewhere than in the preaching. Ellicott puts the same in a sentence, that a man can have no ground of boasting in doing what he must do. Robertson makes the necessity a compliment, that Paul could do no other and deserves no credit for it, having heard a real call, and wishes the same were true of every modern preacher. Clarke turns it into a double warning, woe to the man who runs when God has not sent him and woe to him who refuses to run or ceases to run when God has sent him. Gill draws the distinction the others leave implicit, that Paul might glory before men and against the false teachers but not before God, since the gifts, the courage and the success were all of grace; and Calvin, faced with the places where Paul does glory in his office, answers that the glorying denied here is only the sort a man sets against slanderers.

What willingly and unwillingly mean is the knot. Ellicott states the argument as a supposition: if there were no necessity, undertaking the work freely would earn a reward, but since the necessity is real Paul is merely a steward doing what he was told. Robertson admits the reasoning is not wholly clear, and cuts it by saying Paul's call was plain enough that he worked willingly and had his reward, only that the reward was the freedom of charge itself. Clarke will not settle it and prints two other men's renderings beside his own, from Knatchbull and Wakefield, on which the office is committed without consent and the reward is precisely the preaching free of charge. Gill notes that the case supposed did not exist. Wesley makes the observation that explains the difficulty better than any construction of the grammar: Paul speaks here in a manner peculiar to himself, for another man might have preached willingly and still received a maintenance, whereas if Paul had received anything he would have called that preaching unwillingly; and in the next verse another might have used the power without abusing it, whereas Paul would have called his using it at all an abuse.

That word is itself disputed. Clarke argues that it does not mean abusing but using to the uttermost, exacting everything a man may claim by law, and Robertson agrees so far as the grammar goes, taking the compound in its perfective force as using to the full; Wesley keeps a shade of the older sense and renders it an unseasonable use. Clarke then turns the point both ways: preachers who insist on their privileges tempt people to think they seek secular goods rather than souls, yet the people readiest to think so are those unwilling to grant common necessaries to those who watch over them, and were preachers as sparing of the bread of life as some congregations are of the bread that perishes there would be a famine. Ellicott proposes to remove the question mark altogether and read the verse as one sentence, asking what reward is to be his which induces him to make the gospel without charge. Barnes guards the conclusion twice, that Paul did not give up his support because he had no right to it, and that he does not say others would do well to follow him in it. Calvin closes with the use Rome had made of the passage, that since Paul might have fulfilled his office by preaching and here adds something over and above, works of supererogation are established; he refuses the inference, holding that what is added is not beyond duty but the willingness without which duty is not discharged as it should be.
19:
Gill notices that the word men is not in the original and the phrase may as well be neuter, the freedom being from the curse of the moral law and the yoke of the ceremonial; Barnes allows the ambiguity but holds the connexion fixes it to persons, and Calvin prefers the same. Henry sets out the paradox, that Paul was free-born and depended on no one, yet was careful to please as a servant pleases his master, making himself a servant that others might be made free. Ellicott finds here the answer to the earlier question, that the reward Paul sought was their good. Robertson borrows Edwards, that he refuses payment in money to make the greater gain in souls, and Wesley asks where the preacher is who treads in the same steps.

Clarke and Ellicott agree that the clause denying Paul was himself under the law belongs to the text, Ellicott ascribing its absence to a copyist's oversight. Who the men under the law are is less settled: Ellicott makes them proselytes as distinct from Jews by birth, Barnes another way of naming the same people, Lightfoot the Jews at large as against the Pharisees. Who the men without law are produces the sharpest exchange in the chapter, and it falls between two of the voices here. Lightfoot asks whether the Sadducees or the heathen are meant, tells his reader to inquire, confesses that how Paul could make himself conformable to the heathen is not easy to judge, and allows conformity to the Sadducees in rites but never in their heresy about the resurrection. Clarke names Lightfoot and refuses it on two grounds, that Paul could expect no success among men who denied the resurrection, and that among the heathen he might appear as one who was not a Jew. The rest take the phrase of the heathen without discussion.

The parenthesis that follows is agreed to be defensive. Calvin says it was added to wipe away the reproach with which the false apostles branded the gospel, as though exemption from the Mosaic yoke were a call to licence, and insists the doctrine of Christ omits nothing needed for a perfect rule of living; Ellicott says the same more briefly; Robertson puts it in Evans's phrase, not an outlaw of God but an inlaw of Christ; Wesley extends it, that all Christians will be under the law for ever.

Who the weak are divides them again. Gill and Barnes take them for weak Christians, scrupulous about meats and offended by things lawful in themselves, Barnes describing Paul conforming in dress and habit rather than wound them. Ellicott says we can scarcely read it so, since the whole passage treats of classes outside the Church whom Paul hoped to gain, and renders it that he assimilated himself to the weak points rather than the strong points of Jews, proselytes and Gentiles alike. Calvin sets the limit, that Paul judaized before the Jews but not before all of them, since with the headstrong he would never have been so accommodating, Christ having said to let the blind leaders of the blind alone: we accommodate ourselves to the weak, not the obstinate, and only in things indifferent. Clarke warns those who plead accommodation from this example to attend to the end in view, which was not money or honour but souls, and not ease but increased labour. Robertson draws the same line between principle and expediency, adamant over Titus and yielding over Timothy. Cyril turns the phrase around and applies it to Christ, who comes in various forms to each man for his profit, a Vine to those who need gladness, a Door to those who would enter, a High Priest to those who must offer prayers, a Sheep to those who have sins; he is made all things to all men while remaining in his own nature what he is.
23:
The first verse carries a textual variant and a bolder proposal. Gill, Clarke and Ellicott all report that the better manuscripts read all things rather than this. Clarke then goes further than anyone else and proposes that the word we translate the gospel should here be rendered the prize, so that Paul does all this for the sake of the prize, that he may partake of it with them. Robertson reads it the other way, taking the compound to mean a joint partaker with others and finding in it Paul's evangelistic passion, that he does not wish to enjoy the gospel just by himself. Barnes and Ellicott keep to the common sense, that Paul hoped to share the salvation he preached, Ellicott hearing in the close the personal humility every minister feels as he realises the greatness of his office. Calvin turns it into a warning, that since Paul argues from the design of the gospel rather than his office, he intimates that all who do not act the same part are unworthy of its fellowship.

The Isthmian games supply the figure, and Ellicott supplies the games. They were national and religious festivals; none but freemen could enter; competitors had to satisfy the officers of ten months' training and thirty days at the gymnasium; a herald proclaimed each man's name and country; the victor was crowned with pine or ivy, and returning home entered his native town through a breach made in the walls. Robertson adds that the crown was of pine at the Isthmus, earlier of parsley, and of wild olive at Olympia, quoting Findlay that these were nevertheless the most coveted honours in the whole Greek world. Gill notes that the Corinthians were presidents of these games, so the allusion needed no explaining; he measures the course at six hundred and twenty-five feet, where Robertson makes it six hundred and six.

The comparison limps in one place, and every voice says so. Clarke states the contrast: there only one received the prize though all ran, here all who run receive it. Calvin says the same flatly, Wesley turns it into encouragement that they may all receive the prize of their high calling, and Henry develops it furthest, that there is room for all and none can fail who runs well, yet there should be a noble emulation, a glorious contest who shall get first to heaven. Chrysostom alone guards the other flank, warning expressly that the words are not to be taken as though here too only one out of many would be saved, far from it, but as setting forth the exceeding diligence it is our duty to use; and he reads the turn as a sharpening of the rebuke, a covert intimation that what the Corinthians counted a mark of perfectness is a superfluous labour, not said clearly lest they grow insolent.

On the training the commentators compete in detail. Clarke prints Epictetus at length: would you win at the Olympic games? then consider the preparations, a strict regimen, food you dislike, exercise at appointed hours in heat and cold, nothing cooling to drink and no wine, submission to a trainer as to a physician, and after all a broken arm, mouthfuls of dust, many stripes, and defeat at the end. Robertson gives the same regimen soberly and calls self-control an athletic axiom. Barnes presses that the temperance covered not only unlawful indulgences but many things reckoned lawful. Calvin brings in the coliphium, the strengthening bread on which wrestlers fed. Ellicott sets the contrasts side by side, that in the earthly contest only one obtains while in the heavenly none need fail, and that the one reward perishes and the other does not. Wesley ends with the sting: the moderns only have discovered that it is legal to do all this and more for an eternal crown than the Greeks did for a corruptible one.
26:
The adverb in the first verse is given three or four senses. Barnes says it occurs nowhere else in the New Testament and takes it that Paul did not run without knowing what he aimed at. Clarke offers three meanings together: uncertainly, since only one could win however many ran; ignorantly, as of a man who does not know the course; and without observation, since all eyes were on the runners, and Paul knew that his false brethren waited for his halting and the Church looked on him with anxiety, so that he acted under the immediate eye of God. Robertson keeps it simple, that Paul kept his eye on Christ as Christ watched him. Calvin reports a reading he does not adopt, that some refer the words to full assurance of hope, as though Paul did not run in vain because he had the Lord's promise which never deceives; his own preference is that the point is to direct the course straight so it may not be wavering. On the change of figure they agree: Ellicott notes the shift from running to boxing and that Paul has a real adversary, Wesley calls beating the air a proverbial phrase for missing one's blow, and Robertson explains it as the shadow-fighting a boxer practised without an opponent.

The verb in the last verse comes from the prize-ring, its application disputed. Barnes derives it from the part of the face beneath the eye and renders it to strike so as to make the part livid, or vulgarly to give a man a black eye; Ellicott translates I bruise my body; Robertson mentions the ox-hide gloves that gave telling blows; Gill supports the sense from a story of Menedemus, so pugnacious in scholastic exercises that his opponents never departed without black eyes. What is being struck divides them. Clarke takes the body itself for the enemy, to be mortified by self-denial and severe labour and made the slave of the soul rather than its master. Gill denies this expressly, that it means neither immoderate watchings and fastings nor whipping and lying on the bare ground, but the body of sin, which he equates with what the Jews call the subduing of a man's evil concupiscence. Ellicott insists that the language of the whole passage is figurative and refers not to inflicting pain but to subduing the appetites, whose true position is to be our servants and never our masters. Robertson denies the Gnostic premise outright, that Paul thought his body evil, and borrows the image of chariot horses kept well in hand by whip and rein. Calvin observes that the ancient monks, meaning to obey this precept, slept on benches and shunned delicacies, and yet the main thing was wanting in them.

The last clause turns on two words. Clarke expounds the first from the games, that the herald proclaimed the conditions, displayed the prizes, pronounced the names of the victors and set the crowns on their heads; Ellicott and Wesley both render it that Paul, having been a herald to others, might himself be rejected, and Ellicott adds that the rendering castaway conveys a wrong impression, the Greek meaning one who has not behaved according to the prescribed regulations. Lightfoot pursues the same word into the rabbinic vocabulary, matching it with the Hebrew terms for approved and not approved. Robertson finds the tone the important thing, that it is humbling to see this wholesome fear instead of smug complacency in the greatest of all heralds. Wesley presses it into doctrine, holding that this single text gives a just notion of election and reprobation, since persons are not represented in Scripture as elected absolutely to eternal life, but believers in general are elected to privileges which, if abused, leave those very elect persons reprobate; Paul was certainly an elect person, and would actually have become such had he not kept his body under.
